I am 49 years old and I have been farming since I was 14, so I know this land better than I know my own hands. I only finished primary school, so I don't read books about farming — I learn by watching my neighbors and by remembering what happened in past years. My family has three people: me, my wife, and my son who is in high school. We have 12 mu and a well for irrigation. Electricity for the pump costs money, so I don't waste water, but I also won't let my crops go thirsty when it matters.

I keep 6 mu for wheat and maize because that is our food security and our base income. The other 6 mu I spread among vegetables and stevia so that if one thing fails or the price drops, we still have something to sell. I learned that the hard way in 2015 when I put too much land in chili and the price crashed — we barely got through the winter.

For wheat, I plant in mid-October with an improved variety I buy from the county supply store. After the maize comes off, I rotary till the field, broadcast the seed and fertilizer by hand, and drag a plank to cover it. I put down compound fertilizer as base — about one big bag for every two mu — and then topdress with urea at jointing in March if the wheat looks a little yellow. I never skip that topdress because three years ago my neighbor Old Zhang tried to save money and his wheat was so thin he cried at harvest. I irrigate three times: winter, jointing, and grain filling. I spray three times total — herbicide once, insecticide once, and fungicide once if the weather is wet. I expect about 450 kg per mu if the spring is decent.

Maize goes in right after wheat harvest in early June, sometimes within two days. The window is very tight, so I plant no-tillage — one quick pass to clear the stubble if it's thick, then straight into the ground with hybrid seed. I buy new hybrid bags every year because saved seed doesn't grow right. All the fertilizer goes in at planting — compound fertilizer and a little urea in the furrow — because there is no time for split application in the summer season. I irrigate twice if the summer is dry, but usually the rains help. I spray herbicide and insecticide, about three times total. I expect around 500 kg per mu.

On the vegetable plots, I grow 2 mu of cabbage and 1 mu of cauliflower in spring. I start them as seedlings in a small bed and transplant. Vegetables need more food and water than grain, so I put more fertilizer per mu — compound as base and urea topdress when the heads start forming. Cabbage gets watered five times, cauliflower four times. I spray more pesticides too, about 4-5 times each, because the insects and diseases come fast on vegetables. I expect cabbage to give about 3,500 kg per mu and cauliflower about 2,500 kg per mu.

In summer I have 1 mu of chili, 1 mu of eggplant, and 1 mu of stevia. Chili and eggplant are my main cash crops besides the grain. Eggplant needs the most water — about 6 irrigations — and both chili and eggplant need a lot of spraying. I check them every morning. The aphids come quick, and if you don't catch them early, you lose the whole plot. I spray about 8 times each. Stevia is newer for me — I started two years ago because a buyer from Shandong comes to the village. It doesn't need as much fertilizer, but you have to harvest the leaves at the right time and dry them properly. I expect eggplant about 4,000 kg per mu, chili about 2,200 kg per mu, and stevia about 250 kg of dried leaves per mu.

My son helps on weekends, and my wife and I do most of the daily work. During wheat and maize harvest I hire two or three people for a few days, but for vegetables we manage ourselves because hired labor is 150 yuan a day now and that eats up the profit. I use rotary tillage for everything except maize, which I plant no-till to save time between crops. I am a bit worried about water costs this year because the well seems to be drawing slower, but we will manage. If one crop fails, the others should carry us through. That's why I never put all my land in one thing.
